transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi... yeah, thank you. Um, well, I guess I'm here because... I've been having these times where I just eat, and it's not even really about the food, it's what happens after. Like, after these eating episodes, I just feel so... gross. I mean, physically and mentally just completely gross and so incredibly disappointed in myself. 

I'll be sitting there in my apartment—usually after I get off my shift, I clean buildings for a living so I'm already exhausted and just wanting to relax—and I just think, like, why can't I just be normal? I feel like I should have way more control over myself, you know? I'm 24, I went to college for a bit, I should know better, but I just lose all control. And then the guilt just spirals, and I end up pulling out my journal. I've always kept a journal, ever since I was younger, but lately... the things I write in it after this happens... they're just awful. I sit there and fill pages just tearing myself apart, writing the meanest, most awful things about myself and my lack of willpower, just how disgusting I feel... and it's just becoming this terrible cycle.
After these eating episodes, do you ever try to compensate for what you've eaten by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or doing something else to try to 'undo' the food?

No, no, I don't do anything like that. I know some people do, like, I had a roommate in college who struggled with throwing up, and it was really hard to watch, but I've never... I've never tried to make myself sick or take pills or anything. I just sit there with it. It's like, I eat all that food, and then I just let it sit in my stomach, making me feel so heavy and awful, and I just kind of... stew in it. I feel like I deserve to feel miserable, honestly. So I don't try to exercise it off or anything, either. I'm usually too tired anyway after cleaning all day, but even if I wasn't, I just kind of retreat to my bed with my journal and write out all those horrible things I was telling you about. I just let the guilt completely wash over me and stay there. I guess I just don't even have the energy to try and undo it, I just let myself feel as terrible as I possibly can.
Outside of these eating episodes, how do you generally feel emotionally? Do you find yourself feeling down or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

I mean, generally... I don't know, it's hard to separate it all out, you know? Because the eating thing takes up so much space in my head. But outside of that... I guess I'm mostly just tired. Like I said, I clean buildings, so I'm on my feet constantly, pushing those heavy carts around, emptying trash, scrubbing floors. By the time I get home, I'm just physically wiped out. 

But emotionally... I wouldn't say I feel depressed, exactly. I mean, I don't think I'm depressed. I don't wake up feeling like I can't get out of bed or anything like that. I still go to work every day, I pay my bills. I still like watching my shows when I get home. I used to read a lot more, like actual novels, not just my journal, and I haven't been doing that as much, but I think that's just because I'm so exhausted, not because I lost interest, if that makes sense? 

I just... I don't feel that deep, dark sadness that people talk about when they talk about depression, except for when I'm in that post-eating spiral. That's when I feel really down. But the rest of the time, I'm just kind of getting by, going through the motions of work and coming home. I guess I don't have a ton of hobbies right now, but I still enjoy talking to my sister on the phone on Sundays, and I still like listening to podcasts while I clean. So, no, I don't think I've lost interest in life or anything. It's really just the eating stuff that makes me feel so miserable. The rest of the time, I'm just... regular tired.
How often do these eating episodes happen? Like, would you say they occur several times a week, once a week, or less often?

Well, if I really sit down and look back at, you know, the past several months... it's pretty consistently at least once a week. Usually just the one night, but it's almost like clockwork. I'll be finishing up my shift, and my feet are just throbbing from walking on those hard floors all day, and I'll tell myself I'm just going to go straight home and go to bed. But then I end up stopping at the store on my way back. I'll go in thinking I'm just getting something small, maybe a normal dinner, but I always end up buying way, way too much food. Just bags of it. And then I take it back to my apartment and I just eat it all in one stretch, right there on the couch. 

And like I said, this has been going on for several months now. I honestly can't even remember a recent month where it stopped for more than a week or so. It's like I'll have a good five or six days where I think, okay, I'm doing great, I'm just eating regular meals, I'm not going to do it this week. I'll even feel kind of proud of myself, you know? Like maybe I've finally gotten a handle on it. But then day seven rolls around, and I'm right back in that store checkout line buying all that stuff again. I keep hoping I'll just naturally break the habit, that a whole month will go by and I'll realize I haven't done it, but no... it never skips more than a week. It's just so frustrating because I know exactly what I'm doing when I'm buying it all, but it's like I'm on autopilot and I just can't seem to make it past that one-week mark before it happens all over again.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

I mean, no, definitely not every day, and definitely not most of the day. Like I was trying to explain before, it's really just tied to the eating. I know depression is a big deal, and I know people who really struggle with it, like they can't even function, but that's just not me. Over the past two weeks, honestly, my days have been pretty standard. I get up, I make my coffee—I have this specific brand I really like that I get on sale, it's the only thing that gets me going in the morning—and then I go to work. And work is just work. I'm busy, I'm moving around, I'm talking to the security guard at the front desk, I'm just doing my job. 

I don't feel sad during the day. I don't feel that heavy, hopeless feeling while I'm emptying the recycling bins or anything. I might feel bored sometimes, or annoyed if someone left a huge mess in the breakroom, but I don't feel depressed. It's really only when I have one of those nights where I buy all that food and eat it all at once... that's when the crash happens. That's when I feel just completely miserable and disgusted with myself. But that feeling doesn't last all day every day for two weeks straight. It's intense when it happens, but then I wake up the next morning, and even though I might feel a little sluggish or guilty, I still get dressed and go to work and get back into my routine. So no, I wouldn't say I've felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day. It's just not like that for me. It's really just those specific moments after I eat like that.
During these eating episodes, do you feel like you're not in control of how much you're eating or that you can't stop eating once you start?

Yeah, that's exactly it. It's like... it's like a switch flips, you know? I'll be sitting there on the couch, and I might even have my sketchbook out—I've been trying to get back into drawing, just little doodles, characters, things like that, because I took some art classes when I was in community college before I had to drop out, and I really miss it. So I'll tell myself, "Okay, Fumi, you're just going to have a little bit of this, and then you're going to finish that sketch." I literally have that thought in my head. 

But then I take the first bite, and it's like the part of my brain that was going to draw just shuts off completely. I'll finish whatever I'm eating, like a whole sleeve of cookies or whatever, and my hand is just automatically reaching into the next bag before I even realize I'm doing it. It's so weird because I'm sitting there, and my inner voice is going, "Fumi, stop. You don't even want this. You have sketches to finish." But it's like my hands aren't listening to my brain. I just keep opening packages and eating, and eating, and eating. 

I've tried so many times to just put the food down. I'll think, "Just put the bag on the coffee table and walk away." But I can't. It's like I'm physically glued to the spot, and the only thing I can do is keep putting food in my mouth. I don't stop until there's literally nothing left of what I bought, or until my stomach hurts so much that I physically can't swallow another bite without feeling like I'm going to be sick. It's just... it's the most out-of-control feeling in the world. I hate it so much, but in the moment, I just cannot make myself stop.
Do these eating episodes and the way you feel afterward ever interfere with your ability to function normally—like at work, socially, or in other important areas of your life?

Well, I mean, it's not like I'm completely falling apart or losing my job or anything. I still make it to all my cleaning shifts. I'm never late, even when I've had one of those nights and my stomach is just in knots the next morning. I still go in, I still get the floors done, I still empty the trash. And I still go to these local design meetups sometimes, too. I try to stay connected to that world, you know, just in case I can ever afford to go back to school. 

But... it does mess with me, definitely. Like, the day after I do this, when I'm at work? I'm just so distracted. I'm pushing my cart down the hallway, and instead of just thinking about what I need to do next, my brain is just on a loop of, "Why did you do that Fumi? Why couldn't you just stop?" I feel so ashamed, and it's like I'm carrying this heavy, gross secret around with me while I'm trying to smile at the office workers. It just takes up so much mental energy.

And it affects my drawing, too, which is the part that really upsets me. See, I keep this journal where I try to sketch every day, but sometimes I also write down how I'm feeling. And after an episode, I'll write these really awful, self-critical things in there because I'm just so mad at myself. Then, the next day, or even a few days later, I'll want to sit down and practice my character designs, but I know if I open that sketchbook, I'm going to see those journal entries. I don't want to look at them. I don't want to be reminded of how out of control I was. So I just put it off. I'll tell myself I'll draw tomorrow, and then tomorrow turns into the next day, and I end up not sketching at all for a while. So, yeah, I'm still functioning, I'm still doing the things I have to do, but it definitely casts this shadow over everything else.
Do you find yourself feeling particularly upset or focused on your body shape or weight, especially in relation to these eating episodes?

I mean... not really? Like, I know a lot of people who struggle with eating stuff are super obsessed with the scale, or they're constantly looking in the mirror and pinching their stomach, or they're trying to fit into a certain size jeans. But that's just not where my head is at. I don't really think about my weight that much, to be honest. I don't even own a scale. I threw it out when I moved into my current apartment because it was broken anyway, and I just never bothered to buy a new one. 

When I get upset after I eat like that, it's not because I'm thinking, "Oh my god, Fumi, you're going to get fat," or "You're ruining your figure." It's really just about the act of eating itself. It's the fact that I couldn't stop. It's the physical feeling of being so painfully full, and the mental feeling of just being totally defeated by a bag of chips and a box of cookies. That's what I hate. I hate the loss of control. 

Like, I wear a uniform for work—these dark blue scrubs that are pretty loose and comfortable, which is good because I'm bending and reaching all day. And when I'm not at work, I just wear regular clothes, jeans and t-shirts mostly. I'm not agonizing over how they fit. I'm not standing in front of the mirror crying over my thighs or anything like that. The shame I feel, the stuff I write in my journal that makes me not want to open it... it's all about the behavior. It's about being weak in that moment. It's about how I promised myself I'd only have a little, and I broke that promise to myself again. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm particularly focused on my body shape or my weight at all. It's really just the eating part that messes with my head.

It's the fact that I couldn't stop. It's the physical feeling of being so painfully full, and the mental feeling of just being totally defeated by a bag of chips and a box of cookies. That's what I hate. I hate the loss of control. 

Like, I wear a uniform for work—these dark blue scrubs that are pretty loose and comfortable, which is good because I'm bending and reaching all day. And when I'm not at work, I just wear regular clothes, jeans and t-shirts mostly. I'm not agonizing over how they fit. I'm not standing in front of the mirror crying over my thighs or anything like that. The shame I feel, the stuff I write in my journal that makes me not want to open it... it's all about the behavior. It's about being weak in that moment. It's about how I promised myself I'd only have a little, and I broke that promise to myself again. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm particularly focused on my body shape or my weight at all. It's really just the eating part that messes with my head.

inference.note: The patient meets the criteria for Binge Eating Disorder (F50.2) based on recurrent episodes of binge eating without compensatory behaviors, significant distress regarding the behavior, and a consistent weekly frequency over several months. There is no evidence of depression severe enough to warrant a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F32.0-F32.9) as the dysphoria is primarily tied to the eating behavior and not pervasive, anhedonia, or other core symptoms of depression. No concerns about body shape or weight indicate disorders like Anorexia or Bulimia, further supporting F50.2 as the primary diagnosis.
